content.text:
## Assessment

I reviewed the two human-authored open PRs: [#232](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/232) and its stacked follow-up, [#233](https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto/pull/233). GitHub also lists an automated version PR, #221. **The work is strong and addresses a real release-integrity failure**, but I would request a small correction before merging the pair and a hosted release exercise before calling the new path production-proven.

| Priority | Finding | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Medium — #232, inherited by #233** | An unsealed file uploaded in the current run is accepted when the index supplies **no SHA-256**. The comparison only flags a digest *if one exists*; the test explicitly expects this result. That contradicts the PR’s confirmation claim and the [publishing guide](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/docs/publishing.md:98>). See [comparison](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/pypi_files.rs:243>) and [test](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/pypi_files/tests.rs:146>). | Either require SHA-256 for files this run uploaded, as the stated contract says, or explicitly narrow the contract and documentation. A hashless response is permitted by the [Simple Repository API](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/simple-repository-api/), so this case needs an intentional policy. |
| **Medium — documentation** | [releasing.md](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/docs/releasing.md:114>) still says a partial PyPI upload can be mistaken for a complete release. That is the behavior #232 changes. The [findings register](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/docs/projects/V1-FINDINGS.md:17>) also describes sealing as unfinished. | Update these current-behavior documents in the PR stack. |
| **Low to medium — performance** | File inventory and the sealed-file recheck read each entire wheel or sdist into memory to hash it. See [inventory and recheck](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/pypi_files.rs:90>). Large wheels can cause avoidable memory spikes. | Use the existing streaming digest pattern used by artifact verification. |

### Engineering judgment

The architecture is thoughtful. The release intent, provider observation, preflight, publish, and confirmation stages have distinct responsibilities. #232 removes the unsafe `dist/*` style upload and makes recovery operate on an explicit file inventory. #233 binds downloaded Python files to a manifest, verifies their bytes, and keeps the matrix build job free of registry credentials. The code also removes known credential variables from Python build subprocesses. Those are meaningful security and maintainability improvements.

The cost is considerable complexity: roughly 2,900 changed lines across the stack, with another durable manifest field and more provider state. I think that complexity is justified for partial-upload recovery, but it raises the value of end-to-end evidence. Both PRs currently have **12 passing GitHub checks**. Their tests cover partial uploads, reruns, yanks, index lag, altered bytes, and manifest validation. The repository also enforces a 90% workspace coverage gate. The remaining limit is that the hosted generated workflow has not run; the existing real-registry tests do not exercise every production binding and observation path.

For publishing practice, Cargo metadata and dependency direction are sound, and Cargo performs package verification during publish; its own guide additionally recommends a pre-publish dry run and package-content inspection. [Cargo publishing guide](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html). For npm and PyPI, the generated workflows still use long-lived secrets. Both registries now document trusted publishing with short-lived OIDC credentials; that is a worthwhile future security improvement, especially for a release tool, rather than a defect introduced by these PRs. [npm trusted publishing](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers/), [PyPI trusted publishing](https://docs.pypi.org/trusted-publishers/). Python-only generated releases also remain unsealed and build inside the write-capable release job, as #233 clearly discloses.

**My merge recommendation:** fix the hashless-confirmation contract and stale docs, then merge #232 before #233. Treat #233’s generated workflow as promising but not fully validated until one representative hosted build, partial upload, and rerun has succeeded. I made no repository changes.

I found three additional issues in the current PR stack. I can establish them from the code, but I cannot verify whether Claude previously noticed them: the saved Entire history is unavailable in this session.

1. **High — a Python-only build runs while Git has write credentials.** The generated [simple release workflow](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/crates/callisto-graph/src/templates/simple_workflow.tmpl:21>) gives the job `contents: write` and checks out with persisted credentials. An unsealed release runs the project’s Python build backend in that job. The [build subprocess](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/registry.rs:293>) removes credential *environment variables*, which is good, but a backend can still run authenticated Git commands: [actions/checkout documents](https://github.com/actions/checkout) that persisted credentials keep `git push` working. This is a supply-chain exposure if a build backend or its dependency is compromised. The new credential-free `build-python` job closes this path for matrix releases, but Python-only generated releases remain on the simple route. I would isolate their build too, or make Git credentials available only after building.

2. **Medium — pnpm discovery and publishing disagree.** Workspace detection recognizes either `pnpm-lock.yaml` **or** `pnpm-workspace.yaml` in [npm.rs](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/crates/callisto-manifests/src/npm.rs:625>). The publish selector recognizes only the lockfile in [registry_argv.rs](</Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/pypi-sealed-set/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/registry_argv.rs:161>). Yes. The recurring problem is that Callisto builds a release decision from a workspace that has never been proven complete.

[Release execution](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/docs/architecture/release.md) has explicit `Absent`, `Exact`, `Conflict`, and `Indeterminate` states. Earlier in the pipeline, [discovery returns a list of projects](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/locate/mod.rs:13), while failed reads, invalid membership, and failed manifest opens can all reduce that list or its graph. A smaller graph still looks valid to the planner.

I see five architectural gaps behind the defects:

1. **No release-ready workspace boundary.** [Workspace loading](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/lib.rs:93) returns a `Workspace` after graph construction, but does not establish that every admitted manifest was read and every package’s publish targets and edges were resolved. Add a validation step that produces a distinct release-ready workspace; `version` and release planning should require it. `status` could still display an incomplete scan with diagnostics.

2. **Absence and failure share the same representations.** `Option`, `.ok()`, `exists()`, and admit-all defaults are used for both legitimate absence and failed observation. [OpenContext](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-manifests/src/lib.rs:206) is a clear example. Use `Result<Option<T>, E>` for optional files and explicit states for membership: absent, valid, invalid. A helper can standardize filesystem reads, but it cannot decide the policy for malformed TOML or YAML.

3. **Filesystem paths are assumed to be Git paths.** Discovery permits directory symlinks, while [apply stages workspace-relative paths](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:509). A package path needs validation against the Git checkout and staging rules before it enters a writable plan. This is a distinct property from being readable or inside the apparent workspace path.

4. **Write authorization does not establish a valid write set.** `ApplyPermit` effectively enforces dry-run behavior. [VersionPlan](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/crates/callisto-graph/src/plan.rs:14) is a mutable collection of paths and edits, and apply performs sequential writes before Git staging. That design intentionally permits partial runs, but it makes late path and I/O failures expensive. A preflight should validate every target, path relationship, and required input before the first write; the existing recovery rules remain necessary.

5. **Tests and specs sometimes preserve the unsafe fallback.** The [workspace spec](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/docs/specs/workspace.json:77) explicitly says malformed membership input admits broadly, and tests assert it. More tests of that behavior will reinforce it. The owner first needs to choose the desired failure policy, then the spec and tests can enforce that policy. Fault injection should cover read errors and incomplete graph construction, alongside the existing release-executor simulator.

I would address these in that order. The key design change is a **validated boundary before planning**, backed by typed “missing versus failed” results. That makes an incomplete package roster an error the planner cannot accidentally treat as an empty or smaller release. It is more effective than a blanket lint against `.ok()` or `Path::exists()`, which would flag harmless uses without proving release completeness.

content.text:
I reviewed the newly merged fixes on `main` at `5e8c1696e`, with particular attention to #235–#240. The changes materially improve the architecture: failed reads now surface, workspace loading refuses an incomplete graph, symlinked packages fail early, and subprocess output timeouts no longer look like successful empty responses. The focused workspace and preflight tests passed (12 tests total). I found **no confirmed high-severity regression** in those fixes.

Two issues remain:

1. **Medium — apply preflight does not prove a file can be staged.** [Preflight](/private/tmp/callisto-codex-review-main/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply/preflight.rs:76) checks paths and filesystem writability, but [Git staging happens after manifest and changelog writes](/private/tmp/callisto-codex-review-main/crates/callisto-graph/src/apply.rs:246). An untracked generated `CHANGELOG.md` covered by `.gitignore` passes preflight; `git add -- CHANGELOG.md` then fails. I reproduced that Git result (exit 1). This leaves the partial apply that preflight is meant to avoid. Lockfile refresh can also fail after the writes, so the new guarantee should be scoped to the failures preflight actually covers.

2. **Medium — changeset creation still has a check-then-write race.** [`add` checks for an unused slug](/private/tmp/callisto-codex-review-main/crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/add.rs:226), then later calls [a writer that replaces its destination](/private/tmp/callisto-codex-review-main/crates/callisto-model/src/atomic.rs:27). Two concurrent `callisto add` processes can select the same filename before either writes; one changeset then replaces the other. The new retry loop fixes collisions with files already present, but an exclusive create is needed to fix concurrent creation.

A smaller accuracy issue: [preflight’s probe creates missing parent directories](/private/tmp/callisto-codex-review-main/crates/callisto-model/src/atomic.rs:117), so “nothing changed before the first write” is not literally true when a later target fails. This is **low severity**; it chiefly affects the guarantee and cleanup.

The earlier PyPI missing-hash behavior is now documented as a deliberate rule for **unsealed** builds; sealed file sets require matching hashes. I would treat that as an accepted recovery tradeoff unless the owner wants identical bytes across unsealed reruns. No files were changed during this review.

We did some work that needs a deep level of adversarial analysis like we've been doing:

Four PRs are open as one stack, merged in this order, and each passes just ci locally. #241, #242 and #244 are also fully green on GitHub (12 of 12 checks); #245 was only just opened, so its checks haven't run yet.

#244:
- Ignored lockfile: a library that gitignores Cargo.lock failed every version with E023 after the manifests were written and some files staged. The lockfile is now refreshed but not staged.
- Ignored changelog or manifest: version now stops with E314 before writing anything, naming the file. Codex's first finding is fixed.
- Concurrent add: add now creates the changeset exclusively. Twelve concurrent add processes keep all twelve in the end-to-end test. Codex's second finding is fixed.
- Preflight probe: it no longer creates directories.

#245:
- Shallow clone: inference from commits stops with E315, because a shallow clone silently shortens the commit window.
- Cargo root detection: it now reads inline, dotted and sub-table workspace forms the way Cargo does.
- npm publishing: it detects pnpm-workspace.yaml, errors instead of falling back to npm when it can't inspect a file, and publishes a nested workspace from its own directory.
- NAPI target check: it reads the main package's own manifest instead of guessing root/<name>/package.json.
- Unreadable inputs: bin_names and relative workspace paths report an unreadable input as an error instead of "nothing there".

Two earlier problems are still open:
- Release notes: a missing, unreadable or empty changelog section falls back to gh release create --generate-notes. Failing instead changes what a release can do, so it's your call. Which do you want?
- Nested Cargo inside a root Cargo workspace: the root's members and exclude still decide. So exclude = ["native"] keeps native/ unreleased, as today.

I’ll review the stack at each PR boundary and then its combined head, tracing workspace discovery, version apply, publishing, and the new error paths. I’ll also test the release-notes choice against the current release contract before recommending a policy.

I reviewed the four PRs as a stack through the current #245 head. All four now have 12 successful GitHub checks, and the reported fixes in #244 and #245 are supported by the code and targeted tests I inspected. I would **hold the stack before merging** because nested npm release still has two high severity gaps that the green checks do not cover.

### Findings

| Severity | Finding | Evidence and impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **High — confirmed** | A nested npm workspace declared only in `package.json` can publish from the wrong directory. | Discovery recognizes that declaration, but [npm_workspace_dir](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/registry_argv.rs:195) recognizes only lockfiles and `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. With `web/package.json` declaring `packages/*` and no lockfile, it selects the repository root. The release provider then runs `npm publish --workspace=a` there. I reproduced npm rejecting that workspace at the root and accepting it from `web`. A package-local lockfile can produce the same mismatch in the other direction. |
| **High — confirmed** | npm observation and publication can address different registries. | [Observation](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/registry.rs:516) runs `npm view` from the repository root; [publication](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/registry.rs:562) runs from the selected nested workspace. With no explicit registry URL, a nested `.npmrc` changes the publish destination but not the observed one. I reproduced npm reading the default registry at the root and a different registry from `web`. A same-version package on the observed registry could therefore be adopted while the intended registry remains unpublished. Directory-based platform publication also runs from the root and needs checking in the same fix. |
| **Medium — source-traced, needs a fixture** | Moving a Cargo package between explicit workspaces can break release-commit verification. | [workspace_manifest_candidates](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/crates/callisto-manifests/src/cargo.rs:240) fetches the explicit `package.workspace` path from the **current** manifest. [Release-commit verification](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:478) uses that set for both commits. If the parent names a sibling `old/` workspace and the release commit names `new/`, the parent’s root is absent from the fetched set, and [historical resolution](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_decision.rs:906) errors. Test that migration before treating it as supported. |
| **Medium — existing issue remains** | The durable-write guarantee still has an exception. | [sync_directory](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/crates/callisto-model/src/atomic.rs:111) returns success for *any* directory-open error, including I/O errors, after the rename. #244 improves exclusive creation and the non-mutating probe, but does not close this earlier durability finding. |

The underlying architectural issue is that **workspace ownership is inferred independently** by membership, lockfile refresh, npm publishing, and registry observation. Lockfile presence is useful for choosing a tool, but it is not a reliable definition of workspace membership. Resolve an npm package’s owning workspace once from its workspace declaration, then use that result for command directory, tool selection, observation, and publication. Pin or explicitly validate the registry endpoint so both effects use the same destination. Add cross-layer tests with a lockfile-free nested npm workspace and a nested `.npmrc`; the current tests cover the pieces separately.

My release-notes choice: **generate notes when no changelog is configured; fail release planning when a configured changelog is missing, unreadable, or has no nonempty section for the version.** A configured changelog is an authored release input, so silently replacing it changes the announcement. That policy would require updating the current [release specification](/Users/gabe/Projects/callisto/.claude/worktrees/leftovers2/docs/specs/release.json:284), which explicitly requires the fallback today.

The root Cargo workspace continuing to govern `native/` through its `members` and `exclude` rules is coherent with the stated contract. I found no reason to change that policy in this stack.
